title: How to Photograph Transparent and Glass Products Without Making Them Look Invisible
description: Glass, crystal, and transparent products are notoriously hard to photograph. Here's the workflow that solves it.

blocks.text: Photograph a glass bottle on a white background. Result: it looks like a faint outline against white. Nothing sells.
Transparent and glass products need special handling. Here's how.
Why Glass Is Hard
Glass, crystal, acrylic, and water:

items.text: Show what's behind them (background bleeds through)
Reflect everything around them (studio, lights, you)
Have edges that are hard to see against light backgrounds
Change appearance based on lighting angle

blocks.text: Most sellers give up and use supplier photos. But those come with watermarks and lack brand identity.
The Two-Background Technique
Shoot 1: Product against a dark background (black felt works). Captures edges, highlights, and product shape clearly.
Shoot 2: Product against a white or gradient background. Captures the transparent, airy quality.
Export a transparent PNG from edit-photo, then place it into the final scene or layout with a general design editor. Keep the original and transparent master so the composition remains reversible.
The Backlighting Trick
Position a light behind the transparent product, pointing at the camera. This creates a rim of light around the product's edges—making it visible against any background.
Combined with background removal at edit-photo.com, you get a cleanly isolated glass product that shows its transparency without disappearing.
For Products With Liquid Inside
Perfumes, oils, beverages:

items.text: Show through-view of the liquid color

For Empty Glass Products
Vases, glasses, jars:

items.text: Show reflection subtly (don't remove all reflections—glass needs some)

blocks.text: The Reflection Question
Some reflections make glass look premium (subtle highlights). Others make it look cheap (your face in the shot).
Rule: keep reflections that describe the product's material. Remove reflections that describe your environment.

The current edit-photo tool isolates a foreground subject; it is not a general object-removal or inpainting tool. For unwanted people or objects inside the scene, reshoot, crop, or use a licensed editor designed for that task.
Common Mistakes
Removing all reflections: Product looks fake and flat.
White background with no shadow: Glass looks invisible.
Cluttered background bleeding through: Product looks messy.
Front-lit only: Edges disappear, glass loses shape.
